twist.stem: Each morning Priyanka puts the kettle on, then checks her plant pots without thinking. The kettle breaks, so she boils water in a pan. By night the plants are unchecked. Why?
twist.hint: What came just before the pot check each day?

options.text: Putting the kettle on was the cue, and it changed.
options.feedback: Right. The kettle was the act just before the check. With the cue gone, the check did not start by itself.

options.text: Her wish to look after the plants faded.
options.feedback: Her wish did not change in a day. The cue changed, and a goal alone may not start a habit.

options.text: She chose to skip it, as habits run on daily choice.
options.feedback: A habit needs little choosing. The kettle cue set the check off, and that cue was missing.

transfer.stem: At her new office in Kochi, Deepa eats a biscuit each time she opens her late-morning email batch. She hardly notices doing it. What is most likely starting the snack?
transfer.hint: What happens just before the biscuit every day?

options.text: Hunger that builds up by late morning.
options.feedback: Hunger may play a part, but the snack comes with the emails each time. That fixed moment acts as the cue.

options.text: Opening the emails at that time.
options.feedback: Right. The snack comes with the emails each time, so that fixed moment is working as a cue.

options.text: A fresh choice she makes each day.
options.feedback: She hardly notices it, which points to a cue. A habit set off by a cue needs little deciding.

twist.stem: Mitali has practised sitar after school for two months, and it now feels almost automatic. If she keeps going one more week, what will that week most likely add?
twist.hint: Where on the curve is she now?

options.text: The biggest jump yet, as practice piles up.
options.feedback: Gains do not grow with time. Early repeats add the most, and later ones add less.

options.text: The same gain as her first week did.
options.feedback: The first week brought the big jump. Near the plateau, a week adds much less.

options.text: A small gain in ease.
options.feedback: Right. She is near the plateau, where each repeat adds less and less.

transfer.stem: Joseph joins a bank in Chennai and must learn a new billing screen. In week one his speed jumped. Now, months later, it barely moves. What does the flat stretch most likely mean?
transfer.hint: Which part of the curve is flat?

options.text: He is close to the point where gains level off.
options.feedback: Right. Early repeats add the most and later ones add little, so a flat stretch is normal.

options.text: His practice has stopped helping, so it was wasted.
options.feedback: The early practice built the skill. Later repeats add less, so a flat stretch is normal, not a sign of waste.

options.text: Each day should add the same, so he slipped back.
options.feedback: Days do not add the same. Early repeats bring big gains, and later ones add less and less.

twist.stem: Nitin and his sister start new daily habits on the same day. After a month hers feels automatic and his does not. What fits the study?
twist.hint: Did everyone in the study need the same number of days?

options.text: His habit has failed, as a month is the limit.
options.feedback: There is no set limit. Some people took many months for a habit to feel automatic.

options.text: A gap like that is normal; times varied a lot.
options.feedback: Right. Estimated times ran from 18 to 254 days, so two people can be far apart.

options.text: Hers cannot be a real habit so soon.
options.feedback: Some habits settled in about 18 days. A month can be enough for some people and acts.

transfer.stem: Hetal, a shop owner in Surat, has opened his ledger app each evening for two months. A power cut makes him miss one evening. His nephew says the habit is broken and must restart from day one. What fits the study?
transfer.hint: What did one skipped day do in the study?

options.text: The nephew is right; one miss restarts the count.
options.feedback: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study, so there is no restart.

options.text: The miss is harmless just because he is two months in.
options.feedback: In the study, one missed chance did not undo habit growth. That finding was not tied to being two months in.

options.text: One missed evening did not undo the growth so far.
options.feedback: Right. In the study, one missed chance did not undo habit growth, so he can just carry on.

twist.stem: Aditya finds a ₹200 note on the road in the morning and loses a ₹200 note in the evening. His cash ends the day even. How does the day most likely feel?
twist.hint: Which of the two events weighs more?

options.text: A bit worse than even.
options.feedback: Right. A loss tends to weigh more than a gain of the same size, so the day feels slightly down.

options.text: Just even, since the sums match.
options.feedback: The sums match, but the feelings do not. A loss tends to count for more than a same-size gain.

options.text: Better, since the find came first.
options.feedback: Order was not the point. A loss tends to weigh more than a same-size gain, so the day tilts down.

transfer.stem: Kartik, a farmer near Nashik, is offered an even chance that his crop price lands ₹2,000 above or below a fixed contract. Next year the same deal is ₹20,000 either way. When is he more likely to say no?
transfer.hint: How does the size of the sum change people's choices?

options.text: With the smaller one, as it feels less worth the bother.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. Refusals of fair even-chance deals grow as the stake gets bigger.

options.text: With the bigger stake.
options.feedback: Right. People turn down fair even-chance deals more often as the stake grows.

options.text: Just as often, since the odds are even both times.
options.feedback: Even odds do not make the feelings even. A loss weighs more, and more so at bigger stakes.

twist.stem: Jatin's shares rose from ₹10,000 to ₹14,000, then fell to ₹12,000. He is still ₹2,000 up on what he paid, yet he feels he lost money. Why?
twist.hint: What number is he comparing with now?

options.text: He is below what he first put in.
options.feedback: He put in ₹10,000 and holds ₹12,000, so he is up. The feeling comes from his new start point.

options.text: Feelings follow the final total, not a start point.
options.feedback: The same total can feel like a gain or a loss. It depends on the point he compares it with.

options.text: He now judges from the ₹14,000 high point.
options.feedback: Right. His start point moved to the high, so the drop to ₹12,000 feels like a loss.

transfer.stem: Before appraisals at their Pune office, Rekha was told to expect a 10% raise and Faisal was told 3%. Both get 6%. Who more likely feels the raise as a loss?
transfer.hint: What did each one expect going in?

options.text: Rekha.
options.feedback: Right. She judged 6% against an expected 10%, so it falls short and can feel like a loss.

options.text: Faisal.
options.feedback: Faisal expected 3%, so 6% is above his start point. It likely feels like a gain to him.

options.text: Neither, since 6% is the same for anyone.
options.feedback: The same raise can feel different. Each person judges it against what they expected.

twist.stem: A new study finds losses weigh less than twice a same-size gain. Akash says this proves the pooled figure of about twice is wrong. Is he right?
twist.hint: Did every pooled study land on one number?

options.text: Yes; one study that differs breaks the average.
options.feedback: Figures varied from study to study, so one lower result does not break the pooled average.

options.text: No; figures vary, and twice is the average.
options.feedback: Right. Some studies found less and some more. About twice was the pooled average, so one lower study fits.

options.text: Yes; it shows losses and gains weigh the same.
options.feedback: Less than twice is not the same as equal. Losses still weighed more than gains on average.

transfer.stem: A shop owner in Jaipur is offered an even-chance deal: lose ₹1,000 or gain some sum. Using the average of about twice, what gain would make it feel roughly even to a typical owner?
transfer.hint: How much heavier does a loss feel, on average?

options.text: About ₹1,000, as the odds are even.
options.feedback: Even odds do not make equal sums feel equal. On average, a loss weighed about twice a same-size gain.

options.text: About ₹4,000.
options.feedback: That doubles it twice. A loss weighed about twice a gain on average, so about ₹2,000 would balance it.

options.text: About ₹2,000.
options.feedback: Right. If a loss weighs about twice a gain on average, a gain near twice the loss roughly balances it. People differ, though.

twist.stem: Pallavi hears a flat's rent was once ₹40,000. She knows that is too high, so she adjusts down before making her own guess. Where does her guess likely end?
twist.hint: How far do people move from a first number?

options.text: Still a bit high.
options.feedback: Right. People adjust away from an anchor, but not far enough, so her guess stays near it.

options.text: Right on the fair rent, since she knew to adjust.
options.feedback: Knowing to adjust is not enough. People move too little, so the guess stays pulled toward the first number.

options.text: Below the fair rent, since she overcorrects.
options.feedback: The usual slip goes the other way. People adjust too little, so the guess stays on the high side.

transfer.stem: At a job interview in Hyderabad, Naveen planned to ask for ₹4.5 lakh a year. The recruiter first says, "Freshers here often ask for ₹3 lakh." What is the likely pull?
transfer.hint: Whose figure came first in the talk?

options.text: No pull, since he already had his own number.
options.feedback: A first number can still pull a later guess, even when you came in with your own plan.

options.text: His ask drifts down toward ₹3 lakh.
options.feedback: Right. The first number he heard becomes a start point, and people adjust away from it too little.

options.text: His ask goes up, to stand out from the rest.
options.feedback: Anchors pull guesses toward them. Hearing ₹3 lakh more likely drags his ask down, not up.

twist.stem: In a wheel test, people who got a high random number gave a median guess well below it, yet above what a low-number group guessed. What does this show?
twist.hint: Compare each guess with its wheel number and with the other group.

options.text: The anchor fixed each guess at its own value.
options.feedback: The median guess was well below the high number, so it was not fixed there. It was only pulled toward it.

options.text: The random number had no real pull.
options.feedback: The high group guessed higher than the low group, so the random number did pull their guesses.

options.text: Guesses moved off the anchor, but not far enough.
options.feedback: Right. Each group adjusted away from its random start, but too little, so the groups stayed apart.

transfer.stem: At a charity auction in Kolkata, the host spins a wheel "just for fun" before bidding on a painting. It lands on ₹8,000. What is likely to happen to the bids?
transfer.hint: What do people start from when they are unsure?

options.text: Bids lean toward ₹8,000.
options.feedback: Right. Even a number known to be random can become a start point, so bids drift toward it.

options.text: Bids ignore it, as everyone knows it is random.
options.feedback: Knowing a number is random does not stop its pull. Guesses after a random number still leaned toward it.

options.text: Bids drop, as people distrust the wheel.
options.feedback: Anchors pull toward themselves. A random ₹8,000 more likely draws bids toward it, not away.

twist.stem: Vani lists three reasons a dealer's ₹6 lakh ask is too high. She still offers ₹5.5 lakh, fairly close to it. Did the trick fail?
twist.hint: Recall what the two studies found about the size of the effect.

options.text: Yes; if it had worked, she could have ignored ₹6 lakh fully.
options.feedback: The trick weakens an anchor; it does not erase it. Some leftover pull is what the studies would expect.

options.text: Not really; it weakens the pull, so some stays.
options.feedback: Right. Listing reasons against an anchor shrinks its pull. Some pull can remain, so a close offer does not mean failure.

options.text: Yes; listing reasons just adds to the pull.
options.feedback: Listing reasons against the number made its pull smaller in two studies, not bigger.

transfer.stem: A client tells Shreya, a project lead in Gurugram, "This app should take two weeks." Before giving her own time estimate, what is most likely to weaken that number's pull?
transfer.hint: Which step brings the other side to mind?

options.text: Waiting a day so the number fades.
options.feedback: Waiting was not what the studies tested. Listing reasons against the number is what made its pull smaller.

options.text: Averaging the client's number with her own.
options.feedback: Averaging keeps the client's number in the sum, so its pull stays. Listing reasons against it is what helped.

options.text: Listing reasons two weeks could be wrong.
options.feedback: Right. Listing reasons against a first number brings the other side to mind, so its pull shrinks.

twist.stem: After a month, Lavanya feels sure her new route to college has more traffic. She can recall five jams but none of the smooth trips. What best explains her certainty?
twist.hint: Which trips fit her idea?

options.text: She kept the jams in mind and let smooth days slip.
options.feedback: Right. We notice and recall clues that fit a belief and skip the rest, so the belief feels proved.

options.text: The new route must really be worse.
options.feedback: It might be, but her memory is one-sided. Smooth trips that did not fit were not counted.

options.text: Smooth trips are rare, so she had none to recall.
options.feedback: She had smooth trips but did not keep them in mind. Clues that do not fit a belief tend to be skipped.

transfer.stem: A mother in Patna believes her son's marks dropped because of his new friends. She brings up each low mark after he meets them. What is she most likely leaving out?
transfer.hint: Which results would not fit her idea?

options.text: More low marks from the same weeks.
options.feedback: More low marks would fit her belief. What tends to be skipped are the marks that go against it.

options.text: Good marks that came after he met them.
options.feedback: Right. Marks that do not fit her belief tend to be passed over, so her case looks stronger than it is.

options.text: The low marks already prove her case.
options.feedback: Low marks fit her idea, but so might other causes. Marks that do not fit are the ones she may miss.

twist.stem: Neha guesses a secret number rule is "goes up by 5." Which test would best tell her guess apart from other rules?
twist.hint: Which triple would break her guess if it still fits?

options.text: Trying 15, 20, 25.
options.feedback: These fit her guess, but they also fit many other rules. A fitting case like this proves little.
Bigger numbers that go up by 5 still fit her guess and other rules too, so they cannot tell rules apart.

options.text: Trying 4, 9, 13.
options.feedback: Right. Those numbers do not go up by 5. If they still fit, her guess is wrong, so this test can tell rules apart.

transfer.stem: A cafe owner in Shillong thinks cold-coffee sales rise because of her new sign. Sales went up each week the sign was up, all in summer. Why is that weak proof?
transfer.hint: What else changed in those same weeks?

options.text: Hot weather could explain the rise as well.
options.feedback: Right. Cases that fit her idea also fit another cause, summer heat, so they prove little on their own.

options.text: A few weeks are too few, so more weeks could settle it.
options.feedback: More summer weeks would not help. Each would still fit both the sign and the heat.

options.text: Sales rises cannot be measured.
options.feedback: Sales can be counted. The problem is that the rise fits more than one cause.

twist.stem: A courier office has a rule: "If a parcel is marked Express, it has a red sticker." Which parcel should you check to try to break the rule?
twist.hint: Look for the case that could break the if-then.

options.text: A parcel with a red sticker.
options.feedback: Whatever its label, a red-sticker parcel cannot break this rule. It can only fit it.

options.text: A parcel with no red sticker.
options.feedback: Right. If a parcel with no red sticker turns out to be marked Express, the rule is broken.

options.text: A parcel not marked Express.
options.feedback: The rule says nothing about other parcels, so this one cannot break it either way.

transfer.stem: Mahesh, a farmer in Punjab, believes his field gives more grain when he sows after the first rain. Which record would test this idea best?
transfer.hint: Which record could prove him wrong?

options.text: More good seasons sown after the first rain.
options.feedback: Good seasons fit his idea, but fitting cases prove little. The test is a case that could break it.

options.text: His neighbour's view on the best time to sow.
options.feedback: A view is not a test. The strong test is a case that could prove his idea wrong.

options.text: Seasons sown after the first rain that gave a poor crop.
options.feedback: Right. A strong test looks for cases that could break the idea. Poor seasons after rain would do that.

twist.stem: Shalini is new to Chennai and needs a bus to a temple. A crowd waits at one stop. Her local friend Arul, who knows the routes, is with her. Who is more likely to follow the crowd?
twist.hint: Who knows less about the routes?

options.text: Shalini, since she is unsure.
options.feedback: Right. When people are unsure, they tend to take a crowd's choice as a sign of what is right.

options.text: Arul, since he lives here.
options.feedback: Arul knows the routes, so he has less need for the crowd as a clue. The pull is strongest when unsure.

options.text: Both just the same, as crowds pull everyone equally.
options.feedback: The pull grows when people are unsure. Shalini lacks route knowledge, so she leans on the crowd more.

transfer.stem: On his first day at a Bengaluru office, Gaurav does not know where to keep his lunch box. Most people leave theirs in a cupboard by the door, so he does too. Why?
transfer.hint: What does he not know yet?

options.text: He is the type of person who copies others.
options.feedback: Anyone can lean on a crowd when unsure. It is not a sign of a weak or copycat person.

options.text: He reads their choice as a sign of the right place.
options.feedback: Right. When unsure, we take what many people do as a clue to what is right, so he copies them.

options.text: He fears being told off by the boss.
options.feedback: Nothing points to fear here. He is unsure, so he treats the crowd's choice as useful information.

twist.stem: In Asch's line test, mistakes went from under 1% when people were alone to about a third of answers with a wrong group. What does that jump show?
twist.hint: Was the line task hard when done alone?

options.text: The lines were hard to judge.
options.feedback: Alone, people made mistakes under 1% of the time, so the lines were easy. The group made the difference.

options.text: Most people followed the group each time.
options.feedback: Going along happened in about a third of answers, not every time. People differed a lot.

options.text: The group pressure caused most of the errors.
options.feedback: Right. Alone, almost no one erred, so the extra mistakes came from going along with the group.

transfer.stem: In a team meeting in Noida, the boss and four seniors praise a plan with a flaw that Sakshi spots at once. She nods along. What does Asch's test suggest is the likely reason?
transfer.hint: In Asch's test, was the right answer hard to see?

options.text: Not wanting to stand out from the group.
options.feedback: Right. In Asch's test the answer was plain, so most who went along did it to fit in.

options.text: She must doubt herself, since the flaw is hard to see.
options.feedback: She spots the flaw at once, so it is plain to her. Like Asch's subjects, the pull is mostly to fit in.

options.text: She is a weak person; strong people do not go along.
options.feedback: Going along is not a sign of a weak person. Plenty of people in Asch's test went along at times.

twist.stem: Ten shopkeepers in a market tell Rahul a bridge is closed. All ten heard it from the same tea seller. How much does their agreement add?
twist.hint: Where did each shopkeeper hear it?

options.text: Ten times the proof of one report.
options.feedback: They all heard it from one person, so the ten voices do not add up to ten checks.

options.text: About as much as one report.
options.feedback: Right. Ten people passing on one source is still one source. Agreement is a clue, and this one is thin.

options.text: Full proof, since ten people agree.
options.feedback: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer. Agreement is a clue, so the facts still need a check.

transfer.stem: Hundreds of people in a WhatsApp group say a new coin will soon double in price. What does that agreement tell Abhay by itself?
transfer.hint: Has anyone checked the facts?

options.text: That it is likely true, as so many agree.
options.feedback: A crowd can agree on a wrong answer. Numbers alone do not make a claim true.

options.text: That it is checked, since a big group would spot errors.
options.feedback: Agreement does not mean anyone checked. The facts still need a check of their own.

options.text: That many people in the group say so.
options.feedback: Right. Many voices saying one thing is a clue, not proof. The claim still needs its own check.

twist.stem: Meenakshi is known as the most careful planner in her class. She guesses her thesis chapter will take two weeks. What is most likely?
twist.hint: Think about who in the studies guessed short.

options.text: It takes longer than she guesses.
options.feedback: Right. Short guesses for our own tasks are common, even for careful planners.

options.text: It finishes on time, as careful people guess right.
options.feedback: Being careful does not remove the slip. People in general guessed too short for their own tasks.

options.text: It finishes early, since she plans well.
options.feedback: Guesses for our own tasks tend to run short, not long. Careful planners are no exception.

transfer.stem: Lalitha runs a small tailoring shop in Madurai and guesses how long each of her own orders will take. What do the studies suggest about her guesses?
transfer.hint: Was the slip limited to school tasks?

options.text: They will be right, since this is work, not school.
options.feedback: The slip was found for school tasks and other tasks alike, so work tasks are not exempt.

options.text: They may run short, like guesses for schoolwork.
options.feedback: Right. People's guesses for their own tasks ran short for school tasks and other tasks alike.

options.text: They will run long, to be on the safe side.
options.feedback: Long guesses showed up for other people's tasks. For our own tasks, guesses tended to run short.

twist.stem: Before a three-day trek, Ishita plans each day from the walking hours on the map. Her past treks ran late with rain stops and blisters. Why does her plan look too short?
twist.hint: What slowed her down before?

options.text: Treks are random, so past ones tell her little.
options.feedback: Past treks show delays a new plan has missed, like rain stops. They are useful, not random noise.

options.text: She is weak at sums, so the hours are wrong.
options.feedback: Her sums may be fine. The plan is short because it leaves out the delays past treks had.

options.text: It pictures the ideal day, leaving out past delays.
options.feedback: Right. Plans picture how a task should go and pay little heed to how past tasks went.

transfer.stem: Arjun, a junior engineer in Ahmedabad, plans a report in two steps: write, then send. Past reports all needed his manager's sign-off, which took days. What kind of slip is this?
transfer.hint: What did earlier reports show?

options.text: Leaving out a step that past tasks showed.
options.feedback: Right. When we plan, we picture the smooth path and pay little heed to how past tasks went.

options.text: Bad luck, since each sign-off delay was a one-off.
options.feedback: Every past report needed it, so it is not a fluke. Calling delays one-offs keeps guesses short.

options.text: Too much detail, which slows the plan down.
options.feedback: His plan had too little detail, not too much. It left out a step past tasks showed.

twist.stem: Swati plans to bake a birthday cake. Which record gives her the best guide to how long it will take?
twist.hint: Which source shows how it went for her before?

options.text: The time printed on the recipe.
options.feedback: A recipe time shows how it should go. Her own past cakes show how it really went for her.

options.text: How long her last few cakes took.
options.feedback: Right. How long similar tasks really took is a good guide. Linking past tasks to the plan removed short guesses.

options.text: How long a TV chef took on a show.
options.feedback: A chef's smooth run is not her past. Her own past cakes give a better guide.

transfer.stem: Karan moves to a new Delhi flat. A map app says his office trip takes 25 minutes. A friend on the same road says it usually takes her 50. What gives the better guess?
transfer.hint: Which number is based on what happened before?

options.text: The app, since her trips had bad luck.
options.feedback: Calling her delays bad luck keeps them out of the plan, so his guess stays short.

options.text: Splitting the two, as both are guesses.
options.feedback: Her figure is not a guess; it comes from real trips. Past trips are the better guide.

options.text: His friend's real trips on that road.
options.feedback: Right. How long similar trips really took is a better guide than a smooth-path estimate.

twist.stem: For sleep to help a new memory, which has to happen first?
twist.hint: What does consolidation need to work on?

options.text: Taking in the material while awake.
options.feedback: Right. You learn first, and then the memory firms up over time. Sleep cannot store a lesson never taken in.

options.text: Sleeping long enough that night.
options.feedback: Sleep can help firm up what was learned, but something has to be learned first.

options.text: Hearing the lesson play during sleep.
options.feedback: Consolidation works on what you already took in. It does not supply an unread lesson.

transfer.stem: On her first day at a bank in Mysuru, Anjali watches the cash machine steps once, takes no notes and does not try them. Her friend says a good night's sleep will lock them in. What is the flaw?
transfer.hint: What does sleep need to work with?

options.text: None; sleep locks in anything seen that day.
options.feedback: Sleep can help store what was learned, but it cannot supply what was never taken in.

options.text: Little was learned, so little can firm up.
options.feedback: Right. Consolidation firms up what you took in. If the steps were barely learned, there is little to firm up.

options.text: Memories firm up the moment you see something.
options.feedback: A new memory firms up over time after learning, not at once.

twist.stem: Kunal says sleep after study just pauses the brain, so it cannot help memory more than lying awake for the same hours. What do the studies suggest?
twist.hint: What did the two groups in the studies show?

options.text: He is right; sleep is just a pause.
options.feedback: Sleep is more than a pause. The sleeping brain helps firm up new memories.

options.text: Lying awake helps more, as the brain keeps working.
options.feedback: It ran the other way. Sleep after learning reduced forgetting compared with the same time awake.

options.text: Sleep cut forgetting more than the same time awake.
options.feedback: Right. People who slept after learning forgot less than people awake for the same length of time.

transfer.stem: Rohan, a tabla student, learns a new rhythm at his evening class. Which plan gives it the best chance of sticking by tomorrow's class?
transfer.hint: What did the sleep studies compare?

options.text: Going to bed at his usual time after practice.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep after learning cut forgetting compared with the same hours awake.

options.text: Staying up late to replay it again and again.
options.feedback: More time awake is not better here. Sleep after learning reduced forgetting compared with staying up.

options.text: Watching films late into the night to rest.
options.feedback: A night awake is not rest for memory. Sleep after learning helped people forget less.

twist.stem: After a coding lesson, Sid has a short break. Which use of it is most likely to help him recall the lesson later?
twist.hint: Which break gives the brain the least new input?

options.text: Playing a fast game on his phone.
options.feedback: A busy task fills the break. Quiet rest helped memory more than spending the time on other tasks.

options.text: Sitting quietly with his eyes closed.
options.feedback: Right. A spell of quiet, wakeful rest after learning helped memory more than other tasks.

options.text: Starting the next new lesson at once.
options.feedback: New work right away is another task. Quiet rest helped memory more than other tasks did.

transfer.stem: After a training session on new billing software at her office in Coimbatore, Malini has a gap before her shift. What use of it best fits the rest finding?
transfer.hint: Which choice adds the least?

options.text: Scrolling the news to relax.
options.feedback: Scrolling is still a task that brings new input. Quiet rest helped memory more than other tasks.

options.text: Answering emails, since any break helps the same.
options.feedback: Not every break is equal. Quiet rest helped memory more than doing other tasks.

options.text: Sitting calmly and letting her mind rest.
options.feedback: Right. A brief spell of quiet rest after learning helped memory more than spending that time on other tasks.

twist.stem: Arjun is teaching his new puppy to sit. In the first week, when should a treat come to teach the act fastest?
twist.hint: What teaches a brand-new act quickest?

options.text: After every sit.
options.feedback: Right. A reward after every try is the quickest way to teach a new behaviour.

options.text: After a random number of sits, for suspense.
options.feedback: Uneven rewards keep a learned act going, but a reward after every try teaches a new act fastest.

options.text: After each fifth sit.
options.feedback: A reward on each try teaches fastest. Skipping tries slows the first learning.

transfer.stem: Pradeep, a salesman in Rajkot, makes calls all day. Some calls end in a sale, with no pattern to which ones. How is his reward best described?
transfer.hint: Can he tell in advance which call pays?

options.text: Fixed, since his salary comes each month.
options.feedback: The monthly salary is a different reward. For each call, the sales come at uneven times.

options.text: Variable, since the tries per sale keep changing.
options.feedback: Right. The number of calls before a sale keeps changing, so he cannot tell which call will pay.

options.text: Fixed, since a sale comes after a set number of calls.
options.feedback: There is no set number here. When the tries before a reward keep changing, the schedule is variable.

twist.stem: Anil's cousin sends funny voice notes at random times. His boss sends one report at the end of each day. Which chat is Anil likely to check more often through the day?
twist.hint: Which one could have something new at any moment?

options.text: The boss's chat, since it matters more.
options.feedback: The boss's report comes at a known time, so there is no point checking early. Unknown timing drives checking.

options.text: Both the same, since he likes both.
options.feedback: Liking is not the driver. Not knowing when the next reward comes keeps people checking.

options.text: The cousin's chat.
options.feedback: Right. When a reward could come at any time, people keep checking at a high, steady rate.

transfer.stem: A reporter in Patna gets a big story tip now and then from one source, with no pattern. The source moves away without saying so. What is most likely?
transfer.hint: Can she tell that the next tip is not coming?

options.text: She keeps checking with the source for a long time.
options.feedback: Right. Habits built on uneven rewards are slow to fade, since the next try might still pay.

options.text: She stops at once, since tips were rare anyway.
options.feedback: With uneven rewards she cannot tell the tips have stopped, so the checking fades slowly.

options.text: She stops soon, as uneven rewards build weak habits.
options.feedback: It runs the other way. Responses built on uneven rewards are slow to fade when rewards stop.

twist.stem: Which app feature can stretch time on an app without any surprise reward at all?
twist.hint: Which one has no element of chance?

options.text: A prize box that opens at random.
options.feedback: A random prize is a surprise reward. Apps also use other features, like endless scroll.

options.text: A feed that keeps loading as you scroll.
options.feedback: Right. Endless scrolling stretches time on an app, and it works without a surprise reward.

options.text: A like count that pops up at odd times.
options.feedback: Likes at odd times are a surprise reward. Endless scroll is a pull of a different kind.

transfer.stem: Ankita's grandmother opens a video app each night. Ankita says she is hooked on random rewards, like a slot machine. What else could fit?
transfer.hint: Why do people open apps at all?

options.text: Random rewards explain her app use by themselves.
options.feedback: Apps use several hooks, and people come for many reasons. Random rewards are one part.

options.text: She lacks the willpower to stop.
options.feedback: Willpower is not the whole story. People open apps for many motives, like news or family.

options.text: She may want news, family clips or a break.
options.feedback: Right. People use apps for many motives, and surprise rewards are only one pull.

twist.stem: Kunal's plan: "If I feel motivated, then I will study." What is weak about it?
twist.hint: Can he tell when that feeling will show up?

options.text: The if part is not a clear moment.
options.feedback: Right. An if-then plan names when and where in advance. A feeling that may never come is not a clear cue.

options.text: It has no goal in it.
options.feedback: Studying is the goal and the action. The weak part is the if, which names no clear moment.

options.text: The then part should come first.
options.feedback: Order is fine: if a moment comes, then act. The trouble is that his moment is vague.

transfer.stem: Sneha, who works in Nagpur, wants to save more of her salary. Which line is an if-then plan?
transfer.hint: Look for a named moment tied to an action.

options.text: I will put ₹2,000 into savings each month from now on.
options.feedback: This sets an amount but names no moment to act. An if-then plan ties the action to a cue.

options.text: If my salary lands, then I move ₹2,000 to savings.
options.feedback: Right. It names the moment, the salary landing, and the action that follows it.

options.text: If I can manage it, then I will save more.
options.feedback: This has an if, but "if I can" is not a clear moment. The cue must be a set situation.

twist.stem: For weeks Kavita's plan has been: "If the 9 p.m. news ends, then I iron tomorrow's clothes." Now she reaches for the iron as the closing music plays, before she thinks. What explains this?
twist.hint: Did she have to decide each time?

options.text: She now enjoys ironing more than before.
options.feedback: Liking was not the change. The plan made the response to the news ending more automatic.

options.text: She reads her plan each night first.
options.feedback: She acts before she thinks, so she is not checking a note. The cue now starts the act.

options.text: The plan made her response to that moment automatic.
options.feedback: Right. If-then plans make the named moment easy to spot and the response to it more automatic.

transfer.stem: Neeraj, a student in Bhopal, wants to call his school friends more. Which plan names a moment he is most likely to notice?
transfer.hint: Which cue is a set situation?

options.text: If I board the Sunday train home, then I call one.
options.feedback: Right. A clear, named moment is easier to spot, so the call is more likely to happen.

options.text: When I miss them, I will call one of them.
options.feedback: Missing them is a feeling with no set time, so it is easy to let pass. A clear moment works better.

options.text: In my free time each week, I will call at least one friend.
options.feedback: Free time is vague and has no set start. A named moment is easier to notice.

twist.stem: Pooja made an if-then plan to jog after work, but she missed three days this week. Does that show if-then plans do not work?
twist.hint: What did the studies find across many tests?

options.text: Yes; a real plan would not be missed.
options.feedback: If-then plans help on average, but they do not promise action every time.

options.text: No; plans help on average but cannot promise.
options.feedback: Right. Across many tests, plans helped on average. A cue can still be missed on some days.

options.text: Yes; plans may help with study goals, but not with sport.
options.feedback: The studies covered many kinds of goals. Plans helped on average, though not every time.

transfer.stem: A homestay owner in Kerala makes an if-then plan for replying to guest messages. What is a fair thing to expect?
transfer.hint: What did most tests find?

options.text: She will likely answer each guest message from now on, without a miss.
options.feedback: Plans help on average. They cannot make sure she acts each time.

options.text: No change, as a plan is just a wish written down.
options.feedback: An if-then plan names a moment and an action, and such plans helped on average.

options.text: She will likely reply more often than with a goal alone.
options.feedback: Right. On average, people with if-then plans reached goals more often than those with a goal alone.

twist.stem: Ravi wears socks that do not match to a wedding. He thinks about 30 guests noticed. What fits the T-shirt study best?
twist.hint: Was the wearer's guess too high or too low?

options.text: Some noticed, but fewer than he thinks.
options.feedback: Right. People guessed too high how many noticed. Some may notice, but far fewer than feared.

options.text: No one noticed them.
options.feedback: Some people may take note. The point is that the guess tends to be too high, not that no one sees.

options.text: About 30, as he guessed.
options.feedback: In the study, wearers guessed too high. More likely, fewer people noticed than he thinks.

transfer.stem: Babita wears a bright new jacket to her office in Shimla. She is sure most of her team will remember it. What is most likely?
transfer.hint: Compare her guess with what others really notice.

options.text: Most will recall it, as it is bright.
options.feedback: Even with a striking image, fewer people recalled it than the wearers guessed.

options.text: Fewer recall it than she guesses.
options.feedback: Right. People in a striking shirt guessed too high how many could recall it.

options.text: Bright clothes go unnoticed.
options.feedback: Some people may notice. The usual slip is guessing too high, not zero.

twist.stem: Why does a speaker tend to overrate how much her own stumble stood out?
twist.hint: Whose eyes is she seeing it through?

options.text: Listeners keep track of each slip.
options.feedback: Listeners noticed less than speakers thought. The gap comes from the speaker's own rich view.

options.text: Her memory is worse than most.
options.feedback: Memory skill was not the cause. Her own close view makes the moment loom large.

options.text: She starts from her own vivid view and adjusts too little.
options.feedback: Right. We live every detail of our own moments, so we do not adjust enough for how little others saw.

transfer.stem: At a family wedding in Lucknow, Saurabh sings a song and hits one off note. He is sure the relatives will talk about it. Most just recall a fun song. What explains the gap?
transfer.hint: Compare how the moment felt to him and to them.

options.text: He lived every second of that note; they heard it once.
options.feedback: Right. Our own moments feel huge to us, so we do not adjust for how little others took in.

options.text: Relatives notice singing slips more than most.
options.feedback: Most of them recall a fun song, so the slip did not stand out to them. It loomed large only to him.

options.text: He has a better ear, so his view is the right one.
options.feedback: His view is richer, not more right about others. He saw it from inside and adjusted too little.

twist.stem: Arjun forgets a line in a school play and spends the night on that one moment. His mother remembers the whole show and the stuffy hall. Why does he expect a harsher view than she holds?
twist.hint: What does each of them focus on?

options.text: Mothers are kind, so her view does not count.
options.feedback: It was not only mothers. People in general judged slips more kindly than the person feared.

options.text: He fixes on the slip; she takes in the whole scene.
options.feedback: Right. Dwelling on our own slip makes us forget what else onlookers weigh, so we expect harsh judgment.

options.text: He is right; one slip sinks a whole show.
options.feedback: Onlookers weighed the whole situation, so one slip mattered less to them than he expects.

transfer.stem: Gauri's card machine fails while a queue waits at her shop in Indore. She expects buyers to think her shop is badly run. What do they more likely weigh?
transfer.hint: What do onlookers see that she forgets?

options.text: That she is badly organised, just as she fears.
options.feedback: People tend to fear harsher judgment than they get. Buyers likely see a common machine fault.

options.text: Nobody saw it, so it does not matter.
options.feedback: Some buyers did see it. The point is that they judged it more kindly than she fears.

options.text: That card machines fail at times.
options.feedback: Right. Onlookers weigh the whole situation, so they judge a slip more kindly than the person fears.
